doc.title: Randy Sandke interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997

title: What guitar and piano gave his trumpet and writing
summary: Voicing chords on guitar helped his writing, and rhythm-section playing gave a different perception of the group.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Was your experience with the guitar and the piano, did that help your trumpet improvising?

Well I mean I guess it didn’t hurt, although before I had had a pretty good grounding in harmony. And I think what it’s helped is my writing a bit. For instance in guitar one of the things you concentrate on is how to voice chords with two notes, with three notes, with more notes than that. For instance if you’re a horn player the difference between a C7 and a C9 is negligible because what you play on top of it is virtually the same. But when you play a rhythm instrument there are quite different sounds. Also, I think where it helped was just being part of the rhythm section too. Because that’s really a different head. And that’s why a lot of guys play drums, play bass, play piano or something like that. Because as a horn player you can’t just sort of float on top of everything else. When you’re a rhythm section player it’s a different perception. A horn player tends to hear the whole thing as a unity. And when you’re a rhythm section player you’re always trying to, you’re aware of your meshing your individual sound, what you’re doing, with the others, to try to get this common groove going. In a way it’s a little more work as a rhythm player I think.
You have to find your spot in the quartet.
Yeah. Like you’re always working to make it gel. Whereas as a horn player working with a rhythm section you’re kind of already feeling the totality of it.
